title: Spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)
subject: neurology
setting: Emergency department, stroke unit, neuro ICU
summary: Rapid CT diagnosis, early smooth systolic BP lowering to 140 mmHg (keep 130 to 150, avoid below 130), immediate anticoagulant reversal with PCC plus vitamin K or specific agents, and early neurosurgical referral for cerebellar haematoma, hydrocephalus or deterioration.

sections.title: Recognise and image
items: Sudden focal deficit with headache, vomiting, very high BP or falling GCS suggests ICH, but clinical features cannot separate it from infarction: image immediately.
Non-contrast CT confirms ICH. Record volume (ABC/2), site, intraventricular extension and hydrocephalus.
CT or MR angiography to look for a structural cause (AVM, aneurysm, venous sinus thrombosis, tumour), especially in lobar ICH, younger patients, no hypertension history, or isolated IVH.
Record GCS and ICH score, but do not use severity scores alone to limit treatment.

sections.title: Immediate management and BP
items: Airway: intubate if GCS 8 or less or airway at risk. Admit to a stroke unit or neuro ICU.
Stop all antithrombotics. Send CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, renal function, glucose; establish the exact time of the last anticoagulant dose.

Systolic BP 150 to 220 mmHg (mild to moderate ICH): start treatment within 2 hours of onset, target 140 mmHg (keep 130 to 150 mmHg) and reach it within 1 hour, with smooth, sustained control and little variability (AHA/ASA 2022).
Do not lower systolic BP below 130 mmHg (potentially harmful). NICE: the fall should not exceed 60 mmHg within 1 hour; decide case by case if systolic BP is above 220 mmHg or onset is beyond 6 hours.
Do not rapidly lower BP if there is a structural cause, GCS below 6, early surgical evacuation planned, or a massive haematoma with poor prognosis (NICE).
Care bundle (INTERACT3): glucose 110 to 140 mg/dL (6.1 to 7.8 mmol/L) without diabetes or 140 to 180 mg/dL (7.8 to 10 mmol/L) with diabetes; temperature 37.5°C or below; avoid hypoglycaemia.

sections.title: Anticoagulant reversal
items: Warfarin with INR 2.0 or more: 4-factor PCC (dose by INR) plus vitamin K 10 mg IV. PCC is preferred over FFP. INR 1.3 to 1.9: PCC may be reasonable. Recheck INR 15 to 60 minutes after PCC.
If PCC is not available: FFP 10 to 15 mL/kg IV with vitamin K 10 mg IV (slower, large volume; watch for fluid overload).
Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g doses). If unavailable, give PCC and consider haemodialysis.

Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban): 4-factor PCC 50 units/kg IV. Andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in December 2025 (excess thrombosis in ANNEXA-I) and is not routinely available in India.
Activated charcoal 50 g orally if a DOAC was taken within the previous 2 hours and the airway is protected.

Unfractionated heparin: protamine 1 mg per 100 units given in the previous 2 to 3 hours (max 50 mg). Enoxaparin within 8 hours: protamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin (max 50 mg); 8 to 12 hours: 0.5 mg per 1 mg.
Antiplatelet-associated ICH: do not transfuse platelets unless emergency surgery is planned (worse outcomes in PATCH).

sections.title: Neurosurgery and raised ICP
items: Refer immediately for evacuation (with or without EVD): cerebellar ICH of 15 mL or more, brainstem compression, hydrocephalus from ventricular obstruction, or neurological deterioration.
IVH or hydrocephalus with reduced consciousness: external ventricular drain.

Supratentorial lobar or basal ganglia haematoma 30 to 80 mL: minimally invasive evacuation in an experienced centre may improve outcome (ENRICH 2024); craniotomy may be life-saving in a deteriorating patient.
Raised ICP: head up 30 degrees, analgesia and sedation, normothermia, osmotherapy bolus (mannitol or hypertonic saline) as a bridge to definitive treatment. Do not give corticosteroids.

sections.title: Monitoring and ward care
items: Hourly GCS and pupils for the first 24 hours; repeat CT within 24 hours and immediately with any deterioration (haematoma expansion is early).
Swallow screen before oral intake; ECG and troponin; cardiac monitoring.

VTE: intermittent pneumatic compression from the day of admission; low-dose UFH or LMWH (for example enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily) from 24 to 48 hours once the haematoma is stable. Graduated compression stockings do not help.
Treat clinical or EEG-confirmed seizures; do not give prophylactic antiseizure drugs. Arrange EEG if consciousness is worse than the haematoma explains.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Young patient, pregnancy or postpartum: look for AVM, cerebral venous thrombosis, eclampsia, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction and sympathomimetic drugs (cocaine, amphetamines).
Thrombolysis-related ICH: see the acute ischaemic stroke protocol (cryoprecipitate, tranexamic acid).

Restarting antithrombotics is a specialist decision: antiplatelets can usually be resumed after the acute phase; timing of anticoagulation for AF is individualised, and left atrial appendage occlusion is an option if anticoagulation is unsafe.
India: deep hypertensive ICH (putamen, thalamus) predominates. Labetalol IV is widely available; confirm PCC and idarucizumab stock and pathways in advance, as availability varies.

sections.title: Escalate and prognosis
items: Transfer early to a centre with neurosurgery and neurocritical care if surgery, EVD or airway support may be needed.
Give full active treatment initially and avoid early withdrawal of care based on the ICH score alone; prognosticate after the first days with the family.
Involve palliative care early for symptom control and family support when the haemorrhage is devastating, alongside active treatment until the prognosis is clear.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Overshooting BP: systolic below 130 mmHg, or a fall of more than 60 mmHg within 1 hour.
Delaying PCC while waiting for INR or neurosurgical review, or giving PCC without vitamin K for warfarin.
Using FFP alone when PCC is available; giving platelets for antiplatelet-associated ICH.
Steroids for oedema, prophylactic antiseizure drugs, or compression stockings.
Missing an underlying aneurysm, AVM or venous sinus thrombosis (anticoagulation is still indicated for CVT with haemorrhage).

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes, may repeat; then infusion 2 to 8 mg/min
drugs.notes: Target systolic 140 mmHg (130 to 150). Avoid in asthma, heart block, bradycardia.

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.dose: 5 mg/h IV infusion, increase by 2.5 mg/h every 5 to 15 minutes, max 15 mg/h

drugs.name: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
drugs.dose: Warfarin: INR 2 to below 4: 25 units/kg (max 2500 units); INR 4 to 6: 35 units/kg (max 3500 units); INR above 6: 50 units/kg (max 5000 units). Factor Xa inhibitor: 50 units/kg IV
drugs.notes: Give with vitamin K for warfarin. Recheck INR 15 to 60 minutes after.

drugs.name: Vitamin K (phytomenadione)
drugs.dose: 10 mg slow IV once; repeat if INR remains 1.4 or more at 24 to 48 hours
drugs.notes: Always with PCC or FFP in warfarin-associated ICH.

drugs.name: Protamine sulfate
drugs.dose: 1 mg per 100 units UFH given in the previous 2 to 3 hours (max 50 mg); 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin within 8 hours (max 50 mg)
drugs.notes: 0.5 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin at 8 to 12 hours. Risk of hypotension and anaphylaxis.

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
drugs.notes: Bridge for raised ICP; monitor sodium, osmolality and fluid balance.
